findings.title: Unknown Threat Actor Uses AI-Driven ARTEX to Target South Korean Finance
findings.summary_md: CrowdStrike Intelligence reported a campaign against South Korean financial organizations active from late September to early October 2026 that ended in exfiltrated data. Open directories on actor-controlled infrastructure held Claude Code session histories, ARTEX configuration files and memory files, and the IP 38.244.50[.]120 hosted an ARTEX instance on port 18899 with a Chinese-language pentesting prompt in a Claude markdown file. CrowdStrike assessed with moderate confidence that the actor was likely a Chinese speaker and financially motivated, and observed DeepSeek v4.1-flash as the primary model with GLM-5.3 and Grok 4.6 also in use.

findings.title: From Penetration Testing to Cyber Threat: Beware of ARTEX
findings.summary_md: CERT-EU said it had observed several threat actors using ARTEX, an open-source AI-powered penetration-testing framework, to automate campaigns against targets around the world, and judged similar activity against EU institutions highly likely to have involved ARTEX. The note describes ARTEX as an LLM-driven platform that turns a natural-language objective into tasks for agent workers using real tooling, with a human dashboard and approval queue but no hard technical enforcement of scope. CERT-EU warned that public availability would make automated attacks faster and more frequent; the original author removed the repository in October 2026 after misuse reports, leaving independent forks in circulation.

findings.title: Threat Overview of ARTEX Autonomous Penetration Testing Framework, FLASH-20261113-001
findings.summary_md: The FBI's 13-page TLP:CLEAR FLASH says malicious actors have used ARTEX since at least August 2026 against organizations in sectors including finance, government, technology, defense and healthcare, with some intrusions reaching privileged access in under three hours. Researchers had found more than 1,600 publicly exposed ARTEX consoles in early November; cited campaigns include the theft of personal information from about 67,000 people in South Korea and attempted sign-ins to more than 2,250 downstream tenants through a ConnectWise supply chain compromise. The advisory lists IP and domain indicators, observed reconnaissance and persistence behavior, and mitigations covering external exposure, identity, application controls and evidence preservation.

findings.title: Cyberattack hits the Commission
findings.summary_md: Politico broke the story of the Commission cyberattack on 19 November, reporting that it had potentially compromised swaths of personal data, blocked staff from entering salary and leave information, and prompted an urgent meeting of the Corporate Management Board. An EU official said the Commission believed it had contained most of the attack but that the full extent of damage was unclear. CERT-EU had detected earlier that month that international hackers used the publicly available ARTEX tool, and disruption had lasted more than 10 days, with Sysper and MyPMO restored but Sysper briefly failing again and translation services also hit.

findings.title: European Commission Cyberattack: ARTEX AI Tool Suspected in Prolonged Disruption
findings.summary_md: Security Affairs reported that the intrusion disrupted payslips, leave requests and medical reimbursements for more than ten days, with Sysper briefly failing again on 18 November, MyPMO restored and the JSIS health portal still down on 19 November; translation services were hit on 17 November. CERT-EU's 5 November technical note identified ARTEX as a possible tool, but the article stressed that no public information explained how the attackers entered and that ARTEX was a suspected tool rather than a confirmed method or attribution. It also noted that under Regulation 2018/1725 a confirmed personal data breach must be reported to the EDPS within 72 hours, with affected people informed without delay when high risk applies.

findings.title: European Commission scrambles to contain AI-assisted cyberattack
findings.summary_md: The Register reported on 19 November that hackers using an AI-powered security testing tool had disrupted Commission systems for more than ten days, taking Sysper, MyPMO and translation services offline. It credited Politico with the first report and cited sources saying defenders detected ARTEX, a publicly available framework whose developer pulled the repository in October while forks remained available. The article also highlighted CERT-EU's 5 November warning and an FBI alert finding more than 1,600 internet-exposed ARTEX consoles, with some attacks moving from targeting to privileged access in under three hours.

findings.title: Cyber attack: European Commission confirms data leak from EU Academy platform
findings.summary_md: Agence Europe reported on 23 November that spokesperson Thomas Regnier confirmed EU Academy was affected by the cyber campaign and that names and email addresses of users had leaked, with only external users affected. The platform was taken offline on 11 November and was expected to remain closed until 14 January, while the exact extent of the leak remained under investigation. Users were told through a website message that warned of spam, identity theft and targeted phishing rather than being contacted individually.
